A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Match-Any-Events work, with matching methods, datasets, and experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. Both were inspected through their references; neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original matching and pose-estimation results on ECM, M3ED, and EDS, alongside component ablations, motion-robustness experiments, and event-based reconstruction.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds training-data ablations in Table 3 and qualitative downstream demonstrations in Figure 6.

M1.justification: The event representation, Temporal Aggregation Transformer, token selection, matching stages, and losses are retained. Expanded halting explanations and the newly stated feature stride document the existing design without establishing an algorithm or architecture change.

E1.justification: The existing training and benchmark datasets remain. New Figure 6 extends demonstrated scenarios to HDR matching in M3ED's schuylkill_tunnel and CAD-reference matching for fast-moving objects, presented as a pose-estimation application.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain the same SuperEvent, MatchAnything, VGGT, RATE, and EventPoint comparisons. Concentrate Net remains in the ablations. New Figure 6 reuses VGGT and MatchAnything under additional input scenarios rather than introducing comparison methods.

E3.justification: Table 3 introduces training controls using only M3ED or only E-MegaDepth against the retained combined-data model. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, resizing, input intervals, and reported training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The added dataset-source ablation tests how real versus synthetic training affects generalization to ECM. Figure 6 adds qualitative HDR and fast-motion case studies. Existing component ablations, interval sensitivity, attention visualizations, and reconstruction analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions repeat RANSAC five times and calculate AUC over all resulting errors. Neither adds training-seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: New Table 3 entries report ECM AUC@5°/precision of 11.33/20.25 for real-only training and 52.63/68.04 for synthetic-only training, alongside the unchanged full-model 54.61/68.90. Figure 6 adds qualitative findings. Tables 1 and 2 and the retained motion-robustness results are unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the ponder loss, and attention-complexity expressions remain unchanged. The expanded halting description explains the mechanism already depicted in v1 Figure 2; no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and discussion retain the same claims about zero-shot wide-baseline matching, motion robustness, cross-modal correspondence, efficient processing, and the two datasets. The headline 37.7% improvement claim is unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 interprets the new real-only ablation as limited generalization likely caused by restricted motion diversity, and connects the new demonstrations to dynamic range and motion blur. Section 6.3 corrects the dataset associated with the indoor VGGT explanation from ECM to EDS.

D1.justification: Section 4.4 newly specifies a coarse-feature stride of 14. This is additional implementation disclosure rather than evidence of a changed setting. Hardware, optimization details, training duration, initialization, and code/data access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 4.2 adds three video-transformer references and explicitly attributes inspiration for separable attention to that literature. Section 4.3 more explicitly identifies ACT as inspiration, although ACT was already cited in v1. The broader research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: v2 makes local grammar and terminology corrections, expands method explanations, renames the reconstruction paragraph to downstream applications, and adds acknowledgments. The main section order and narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 6, restructures Table 3 into module and dataset ablations, explains Table 1's color coding, and enlarges and labels the reconstruction display. Existing figures are also relocated or renumbered; their underlying analyses are retained.

improvement.justification: Table 3 provides useful additional evidence for synthetic supervision, while clearer prior-work attribution and the stride disclosure improve transparency. Figure 6 broadens the demonstrated applications, but remains qualitative and sparsely documented. The ablation prose still misidentifies rows II/III. Overall, these are useful, limited improvements to an otherwise scientifically stable paper.
